---
title: "Introducing anvil: Fast Numerical Computing for R"
date: today
format: html
---

We are happy to announce the initial release of [anvil](https://r-xla.github.io/anvil/), a code transformation framework for R that makes numerical programs fast.
You write plain R functions, and anvil compiles them for high-speed execution on CPU or GPU through the [OpenXLA](https://openxla.org/) compiler infrastructure.
It also provides automatic differentiation, so you can compute gradients without deriving them by hand.
If you have used [JAX](https://jax.readthedocs.io/) in Python, anvil should feel familiar.

This is an initial release, so expect rough edges.
Many features are still missing and the set of built-in operations will continue to grow.
We are releasing early because we believe the core functionality is already useful and we want to gather feedback from the community.
If you run into problems or have ideas for what to add next, please open an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/r-xla/anvil/issues).

You can install anvil from [r-universe](https://r-xla.r-universe.dev/builds) or directly from GitHub with `pak::pak("r-xla/anvil")`.
The [Get Started vignette](https://r-xla.github.io/anvil/articles/anvil.html) walks through a complete example, from creating tensors to training a linear model with gradient descent, and the full API is documented on the [package website](https://r-xla.github.io/anvil/).

## JIT Compilation

The central idea of anvil is that you write ordinary R functions and then hand them to `jit()`, which compiles them into optimized executables via the XLA compiler.
The compiled code runs much faster than interpreted R, because the compiler can see the entire computation at once and apply optimizations such as operator fusion and efficient memory layout.
Once compiled for a given set of input shapes and types, the result is cached, so repeated calls pay no compilation overhead.

## Hardware Backends

The same anvil code runs on CPU and GPU without modification.
Under the hood, anvil delegates execution to the [PJRT](https://github.com/r-xla/pjrt) runtime, which provides platform-specific plugins.
Switching backends is a matter of configuration, not code changes.
This makes it possible to develop and test on a laptop and then scale to GPU hardware when needed.

## Automatic Differentiation

anvil implements backward-mode automatic differentiation.
Given a function with a scalar output, `gradient()` returns a new function that computes the gradient with respect to a chosen subset of its arguments.
This transformation composes naturally: you can define a loss function in plain R, derive its gradient, and build an optimization loop -- all without leaving R or writing any mathematical derivations by hand.
This is particularly useful for gradient-based optimization, such as fitting Bayesian models or training neural networks.
